# Mental status examination

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Basics of neurology > Mental status examination*

[Original Article Link](/library/br0Hfh)

---

## Summary

The mental status examination (<u>MSE</u>) is an important diagnostic tool in both neurological and psychiatric practice. <u>MSE</u> is used to describe a patient's mental state and behaviors, both quantitatively and qualitatively, at a specific point in time. The main components of an <u>MSE</u> are <u>appearance and behavior</u>, <u>mood and affect</u>, speech, <u>thought process</u> and content, <u>perceptual disturbances</u>, sensorium and <u>cognition</u>, and insight and judgment. The clinician conducting an <u>MSE</u> collects data by observing the interviewed individual's behavior and asking specific questions. The findings of the <u>MSE</u> summarize the results of a psychiatric examination on a comprehensive, cross-sectional level. When integrated with the interviewee's biographical information and psychiatric history, <u>MSE</u> findings form the basis for diagnostic and therapeutic decisions. A thorough <u>MSE</u> also provides essential information for establishing a diagnosis according to <u>DSM-5</u> criteria.




When conducting the <u>MSE</u> or interpreting <u>MSE</u> findings, it is important to consider the cultural background of both the clinician conducting the <u>MSE</u> and the interviewee because behavioral patterns vary significantly across cultures (e.g., nodding your head as a sign of approval in some countries might signify disagreement in others). Other factors that should be taken into account when conducting an <u>MSE</u> include the religious, educational, and social backgrounds of the interviewed individuals. Similarly, the clinician should be aware of any potential language barriers. The <u>MSE</u> is not to be confused with the <u>Mini-Mental State Examination</u> (<u>MMSE</u>), which is a screening tool for <u>dementia</u> but can also be used as part of the <u>MSE</u> to assess sensorium and <u>cognition</u>.

---

## General structure

The <u>MSE</u> is composed of the following components: [[1]](/library/WibPqt)




* <u>Appearance and behavior</u>

* Sensorium and <u>cognition</u>

* <u>Mood and affect</u>

* Speech

* <u>Thought process</u>

* <u>Thought content</u>

* <u>Perceptual disturbances</u>

* Insight and judgment

---

## Appearance and behavior

### Appearance




* Abnormalities in appearance can provide insight into an individual's lifestyle and ability to care for themselves.

* Such abnormalities can be the first indicator of a number of psychiatric conditions.

* Individuals with severe <u>depression</u> may present with <u>significant weight loss</u> or appear disheveled.

* A patient with <u>histrionic personality disorder</u> might wear what is considered an inappropriately seductive outfit or excessive makeup, either in the context of the patient's cultural norms or in contrast to how they dressed previously.

* An individual that is currently experiencing a <u>manic</u> or <u>hypomanic episode</u> may present with extremely colorful <u>hair</u> or dress in brightly colored or flamboyant clothing.

* Needle marks or <u>jaundice</u> could indicate <u>substance abuse</u>.

* When assessing a patient's physical appearance, a physician should pay attention to the following features:

* Estimated age by physical appearance: should be compared with the patient's stated age

* Body habitus

* Bodyweight (e.g., the patient is <u>obese</u> or underweight)

* Physical abnormalities (e.g., <u>marfanoid habitus</u> )

* Posture (e.g., open or closed, tense or relaxed)

* Hygiene

* Level of grooming (e.g., meticulously shaved or excessively scruffy)

* Presence of body odor and/or <u>halitosis</u>

* Dress: the amount and type of clothing used by the patient, taking into consideration the patient's cultural norms

* Distinguishing features

* Wounds (e.g., <u>burns</u>, scratches, needle marks) and/or scars

* Tattoos and/or body piercings

* Dental <u>braces</u>, jewelry, glasses





### Behavior




* Similar to appearance, the assessment of an individual's behavior can also provide important clues for establishing a diagnosis.

* <u>Psychomotor agitation</u> is commonly observed in individuals experiencing <u>mania</u>, whereas psychomotor retardation is usually seen in individuals with <u>depression</u>.

* Glancing repeatedly at different parts of the room is commonly seen in individuals experiencing auditory or <u>visual hallucinations</u> (e.g., in <u>schizophrenia</u>).

* Abnormal motor activity (movements, gait) can be a sign of an underlying neurological disorder or a side effect of <u>psychotropic medication</u>.

* A physician should pay attention to the following aspects of an individual's behavior:

* <u>Eye</u> contact

* Level of <u>eye</u> contact (e.g., none, decreased, normal, increased)

* Type of <u>eye</u> contact (e.g., fleeting, intrusive)

* Attitude toward the interviewer (e.g., friendly, cooperative, indifferent, evasive, defensive, seductive)

* Level of <u>distress</u> (e.g., mild, moderate, severe)

* Disorders of diminished motivation (<u>DDM</u>): characterized by impairment in goal-directed behavior, thought, and emotion [[2]](/library/h4bcQF)

* Because they are not classified as disorders within <u>DSM-5</u>, it is uncertain if they are distinct disorders or symptoms that overlap with other conditions.

* There are three types that vary in severity:

* Apathy: the least severe form of <u>DDM</u> characterized by reduced motivation and/or goal-directed behavior

* Abulia: a more severe form of <u>DDM</u> characterized by diminished in purposeful movements, will, and/or initiative

* Akinetic mutism: the most severe form of <u>DDM</u> characterized by the absence of movements and paucity of speech determined by lack of motivation





#### Abnormal motor activity




* Abnormal movements: See “<u>Examination of the motor system</u>” and “<u>Muscle appearance</u>” in <u>neurological examination</u>.

* Gait: See <u>gait assessment</u> in <u>neurological examination</u> for more information.

* Apraxia: difficulty performing targeted, voluntary movements despite an intact <u>motor function</u> and the willingness to perform the movement

* Ideomotor apraxia: difficulty imitating actions; mismatch between intention and expression (e.g., instead of waving, a patient will scratch his <u>ear</u>)

* Ideational apraxia: difficulty planning and completing multistep actions when interacting with objects

* Constructional apraxia: difficulty drawing or creating objects out of different parts

* Apraxia of lid opening: difficulty voluntarily opening the eyes in the absence of <u>levator palpebrae</u> muscle palsy

---

## Sensorium and cognition

### Sensorium




* The evaluation of sensorium assesses a patient's <u>level of consciousness</u> and their <u>orientation to person, place, and time</u>.

* Because sensorium impairments can have vital implications, the evaluation of sensorium should be performed at the beginning of the <u>MSE</u>.





#### Orientation to person, place, and time




* Can be assessed by asking the patient their full name, the current date, and the current location

* Disorientation is a state characterized by the loss of the notion of time, place, and/or space.

* Awareness to time is lost first, followed by orientation to place, and lastly to self.

* Common causes include:

* <u>Hypoxia</u>

* <u>Vitamin deficiencies</u>

* Infections

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>

* <u>Head trauma</u>

* <u>Dehydration</u>

* <u>Substance abuse</u>





#### Level of consciousness




* <u>Level of consciousness</u> is a person's level of <u>arousability</u> and response to external stimuli (e.g., verbal, painful stimuli).

* It is typically assessed by evaluating the patient's response to external stimuli and can be described using the following:

* Alertness (consciousness)

* A state of awareness of oneself and the surrounding environment

* Considered a normal finding

* Somnolence

* A state of drowsiness from which a patient can be easily aroused

* The patient responds normally except for a slight delay when addressed.

* Lethargy

* A state of impaired consciousness and drowsiness from which the patient can be awoken if exposed to moderate stimuli [[3]](/library/SibyIt)

* The patient has decreased interest in the surrounding environment and tends to fall back asleep after being aroused.

* Obtundation

* A state of impaired consciousness characterized by increased sleepiness and a slow response to external stimuli

* Similar to <u>lethargy</u>, the patient has a decreased interest in the surrounding environment and experiences drowsiness between the sleeping episodes.

* Stupor

* A state of insensitivity bordering on unconsciousness;  from which the patient is not easily awoken, except if exposed to strong external stimuli,;  (e.g., sternal rub) and into which the patient returns in the absence of further stimulation

* Communication is not possible and a painful stimulus provokes a withdrawal response.

* Coma

* A state of complete unarousable unresponsiveness regardless of the stimulus, typically lasting for 2–4 weeks [[4]](/library/hibcrt)

* A <u>comatose</u> state is characterized by closed eyes and decreased/absent reflex responses and motor activity, but preserved circulatory function and breathing drive.

* <u>Delirium</u>

* A <u>transient loss of consciousness</u>, cognitive function, and psychomotor behavior that is usually the result of an underlying medical condition (e.g., <u>acute kidney injury</u>)

* See <u>delirium</u> for more information.

* A quantitative assessment of consciousness is more likely to be used in clinical settings because it provides a more objective assessment of the patient's <u>level of consciousness</u>.

* Glasgow <u>Coma</u> Scale (<u>GCS</u>): A standardized scoring scale used for the evaluation of consciousness in acute settings (especially after <u>head injury</u>) and sometimes for monitoring patients in the <u>ICU</u>.

* The scale scores the patient's <u>eye</u> response (1–4 points), verbal response (1–5 points), and motor response (1–6 points).

* A maximum score of 15 points indicates full consciousness, while a minimum score of 3 points can indicate deep <u>coma</u> or <u>brain death</u>.

* See “Diagnostics” in <u>traumatic brain injury</u> for more information.





### Cognition




<u>Cognition</u> is the mental process of gaining knowledge and understanding via thinking, experiencing, and sensing, and includes many aspects listed below. The assessment of cognitive function during an <u>MSE</u> is usually performed using screening tools such as the <u>MMSE</u> and/or the <u>Saint Louis University Mental Status Examination</u> (<u>SLUMS</u>). (See “<u>Cognitive assessment</u>” in <u>major neurocognitive disorder</u> for more information.)




* Attention (cognition) and concentration

* The ability of an individual to focus and sustain their thoughts on a specific task/topic

* Can be assessed by asking the patient to spell a word backward or count in twos

* <u>Memory (cognition)</u>

* The process of recalling information

* Classified according to the length of time a particular piece of information can be recalled.

* <u>Sensory (immediate) memory</u> (registration)

* The shortest type of information storage

* Can be assessed by asking the patient to repeat a set of numbers or words in the original order

* <u>Short-term memory</u>

* Information is stored for a few minutes in order to be processed and used while performing a task

* Can be assessed by asking the patients to look at a set of numbers/words/images for a couple of seconds, and then asking them to recall the items 5 minutes later

* <u>Long-term memory</u>

* Information is stored for days to years

* Can be assessed by asking the patient about an objectively verifiable personal or historical fact (e.g., date of marriage, a former president's name)

* <u>Amnesia</u>: loss of <u>memory</u>

* <u>Retrograde amnesia</u>: inability to recall memories and/or information acquired prior to the incident

* <u>Anterograde amnesia</u>: inability to recall memories and/or information acquired after the incident

* <u>Global amnesia</u>: inability to recall memories and/or information acquired prior to and after the incident

* Confabulation: filling in <u>lapses</u> of <u>memory</u> with fabricated events, without the intention of deceiving the interviewer

* Calculation

* The ability to perform simple calculations, according to the patient's level of education

* Can be assessed by asking the patient to continuously subtract 7 starting from 100

* Acalculia: inability to perform simple calculations (usually a sign of <u>parietal lobe</u> lesions)

* Language: see “Language” section below.

* Fund of knowledge

* The amount of general information an individual stores in their long-term <u>memory</u>

* Can increase with education; decreases in a number of conditions (e.g., <u>dementia</u>)

* Can be assessed by asking the patient to name the last five presidents or the state capital

* Abstract reasoning

* The ability to analyze information, detect patterns and connections between different pieces of data, and apply that knowledge to practice

* Can be assessed by asking the patient to find the similarities between objects (e.g., the similarities between a triangle and a square)

* Executive function

* A set of cognitive functions that allows an individual to plan, evaluate, and execute new and complex tasks

* Can be assessed by using <u>neuropsychological tests</u>, such as the <u>Wisconsin Card Sorting Test</u> or the <u>clock drawing test</u> [[5]](/library/3ibSrt)

## Speech

* Speech is the spontaneous production of the spoken language (i.e., the act of speaking ) and is characterized by the following:

* Rate: rapid, normal, slow, or pressured

* Volume: loud, normal, soft, or whispered

* Quantity: <u>logorrheic</u>, talkative, responsive, or reserved

* Articulation and fluency: incomprehensible, accented, stuttered, lisping, mumbled, slurred, clear, or articulated

* Speech latency: increased, decreased, or no latency

* Because speech impairment is characteristic of a large number of conditions, it is an important diagnostic tool.

* Individuals with <u>depression</u> may have soft, almost incomprehensible speech with increased latency.

* Individuals in a <u>manic</u> state are often <u>logorrheic</u> and speak loudly and extremely fast.

* Individuals with <u>schizophrenia</u> usually have disorganized, incomprehensible speech.

* Some of the speech abnormalities that can be observed during an <u>MSE</u> include:

* Mutism: an inability to speak that is caused by a structural or motor dysfunction of the <u>vocal apparatus</u> or that is the result of an individual's unwillingness to speak despite having an intact <u>vocal apparatus</u> (e.g., <u>akinetic mutism</u>)

* Dysarthria: the impaired articulation of words resulting from motor dysfunction of the <u>vocal apparatus</u>

* Echolalia: the involuntary repetition of another person's speech

* Palilalia: the involuntary repetition of words or phrases with increasing rapidity

* Alogia/<u>poverty of speech</u>: impaired thinking that manifests with reduced speech output (e.g., always replying to questions with one-word answers)

* Pressured speech: accelerated thoughts that are expressed as rapid, loud, and voluminous speech often in the absence of social stimulation

* Neologisms: the creation and use of new words that are only understood by the speaker (e.g., Pepsidiction = Pepsi + addiction, Spritependency = Sprite + dependency)

* Word salad: incoherent thinking expressed as a sequence of words without a logical connection

* Characteristic of <u>schizophrenia</u> and <u>dementia</u>

* Example: “They’re destroying too many cattle and oil just to make soap. If we need soap when you can jump into a pool of water, and then when you go to buy your gasoline, my folks always thought they should get pop but the best thing to get is motor oil and money.” [[6]](/library/diboqt)

---

## Thought process

* <u>Thought process</u> is the act of thinking and is characterized by the number of thoughts as well as their flow and coherence.

* A physician evaluates a patient's <u>thought process</u> by analyzing the patient's responses to different types of questions when taking their <u>medical history</u> or during their <u>physical examination</u>.

* When describing an individual's <u>thought process</u>, the following terms can be used:





| <u>Thought processes</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description | Characteristic of | Example |
| Circumstantial thought process | <br>* Nonlinear thought expressed as long-winded explanations and with multiple deviations from the central topic before a central idea is finally expressed<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Schizophrenia</u><br><br>* <u>Bipolar disorder</u><br><br>* <u>Epilepsy</u><br><br>* <u>Intellectual disability</u><br><br>* <u>Developmental delay</u> [[7]](/library/VibGqt)<br><br><br> | <br>* When a patient is asked where they are from, they describe their favorite hometown diners before answering your question.<br><br> |
| Tangential thought process | <br><br>* Nonlinear thought expressed as a gradual deviation from a focused idea or question.<br><br>* The patient provides multiple, unnecessary details related to the question without actually answering the question.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Schizophrenia</u><br><br>* <u>Anxiety</u><br><br>* <u>Delirium</u> [[8]](/library/eibxqt)<br><br><br> | <br>* When asked about their <u>medical history</u>, the patient describes the hospitals they have stayed in without mentioning their medical conditions.<br><br> |
| Derailment | <br>* Incoherent thinking expressed as illogical, sudden, and frequent changes of topic<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Schizophrenia</u><br><br>* Other <u>psychotic disorders</u> [[9]](/library/UibbIt)<br><br><br> | <br>* When asked about their job, the patient remembers some funny stories from their childhood and then starts talking about the weather.<br><br> |
| Flight of ideas | <br>* The quick succession of thoughts usually expressed as a continuous flow of rapid speech and abrupt changes in topic<br><br> | <br>* <u>Bipolar disorder</u> (<u>manic phase</u>)<br><br> | <br>* When asked how they are feeling, the patient delivers a 10-minute monologue on different topics using rapid, intangible speech.<br><br> |
| Clang associations | <br>* The use of words based on rhyme patterns rather than meaning<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Schizophrenia</u><br><br>* <u>Manic</u> states [[10]](/library/2ibTIt)<br><br><br> | <br>* When asked “Have you ever smoked?” the patient responds with “Never have I ever, never never ever.”<br><br> |
| Perseveration | <br>* The inappropriate repetition or persistence of behavior, speech, or sounds<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Psychoses</u><br><br>* <u>Epilepsy</u><br><br>* <u>Dementia</u><br><br>* <u>Parkinson disease</u><br><br>* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u><br><br>* <u>Stroke</u> [[11]](/library/fibkIt)<br><br><br> | <br>* When asked three different questions, the patient gives the same answer each time.<br><br> |
| Thought blocking | <br>* The abrupt ending of a <u>thought process</u> expressed as a sudden interruption in speech<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Schizophrenia</u><br><br>* Other <u>psychoses</u> [[12]](/library/Tib6It)<br><br><br> | <br>* The patient stops in the middle of answering a question<br><br> |

## Thought content

* <u>Thought content</u> refers explicitly to what an individual is thinking about (i.e., main themes and beliefs) and is usually evaluated based on the presence of <u>delusions</u>, <u>obsessions</u>, <u>compulsions</u>, <u>phobias</u>, and <u>homicidal</u> or <u>suicidal ideation</u>.

* Important because a large number of psychiatric conditions are associated with various disturbances of <u>thought content</u>, some of which are <u>pathognomonic</u> (e.g., <u>suicidal ideation</u> for patients with severe <u>depression</u>)

* Consider the individual's social, cultural, and educational background, since the understanding of normality varies among these things.





### Delusions




* Definition: fixed, false beliefs that are maintained despite being contradicted by reality or rational arguments and are not related to one's religious beliefs or culture

* All <u>delusions</u> can be classified as either:

* Bizarre delusions: <u>delusions</u> that cannot be true or are inconsistent with the patient's social and cultural norms (e.g., a patient insisting that they can fly)

* Nonbizarre delusions: <u>delusions</u> that could be true or are consistent with the patient's social and cultural norms (e.g., a patient insisting that they have won the lottery when this is not the case)

* Based on their <u>mood congruence</u>, <u>delusions</u> can be classified as either:

* Mood congruent <u>delusions</u>: the content of <u>delusions</u> is consistent with the patient's current mood (e.g., a <u>manic</u> patient insisting they have special powers)

* Mood incongruent <u>delusions</u>: the content of <u>delusions</u> is not consistent with the patient's current mood (e.g., a patient having a <u>manic episode</u> insisting that a murderer is chasing them)





| <u>Delusions</u> according to their content |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Description | Assess by asking patient if they: |
| Persecutory delusions | <br>* The patient insists that they are being cheated on, conspired against, or harassed.<br><br> | <br>* Feel wronged or threatened by a person or group of individuals<br><br> |
| Paranoia | <br>* The patient has an irrational distrust of others and is suspicious of their motives.<br><br> | <br>* Sometimes have the feeling that a person or group of individuals wants to harm them<br><br> |
| Grandiosity | <br>* The patient insists that they have special powers or importance (e.g., a patient saying they can read minds).<br><br> | <br>* Feel like they are destined for something special or have special abilities<br><br> |
| Erotomania | <br>* The patient believes that other individuals are in love with them (e.g., a patient claiming a famous actress is sending them love letters).<br><br> | <br>* Have a special someone who is in love with them and sending secret messages<br><br> |
| Jealousy | <br>* The patient believes their partner is unfaithful without justification.<br><br> | <br>* Have the feeling that their partner is unfaithful to them<br><br> |
| Delusion of reference | <br>* The patient believes that normal events are of special importance to them (e.g., an individual might feel that a television reporter is talking about them).<br><br> | <br>* Have the feeling that people on the street, on the <u>radio</u>, or on TV are talking about them and trying to send them messages<br><br> |
| Somatic delusions | <br>* The patient believes there is something abnormal about their body function or appearance (e.g., an individual might feel like they are missing a hand).<br><br> | <br>* Think that there is something wrong with a part of their body<br><br> |
| Religious delusions | <br>* The patient believes they have divine powers, receive messages from God, or that they actually are God.<br><br> | <br>* Have been in contact with a religious figure or have a spiritual mission of some sort<br><br> |
| Delusion of poverty | <br>* The patient believes they are financially incapacitated or that poverty is inevitable.<br><br> | <br>* The feeling that they are in some financial trouble<br><br> |
| Delusion of guilt | <br>* The patient believes that they have wronged someone and/or are responsible for something bad.<br><br> | <br>* The feeling that they harmed someone or have done something bad<br><br> |
| Mixed delusions | <br>* The simultaneous occurrence of two or more <u>delusions</u>; neither <u>delusion</u> is predominant<br><br> | <br>* See above<br><br> |
| Unspecified delusion | <br>* A type of <u>delusion</u> that does not fit the criteria of other types or that cannot be clearly defined<br><br> | <br>* N/A<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> To remember the different types of <u>delusions</u> (Grandiosity, Erotomanic, Ideas of reference, <u>Paranoid</u>, <u>Persecutory</u>, Somatic, <u>Jealousy</u>), think: “Grand, Erotic Ideas can cause <u>Paranoia</u>, Persecution and So much (so-ma-<u>tic</u>) <u>Jealousy</u>.”




### Suicidal and <u>homicidal ideation</u>




* <u>Suicidal ideation</u>: any type of thoughts that an individual has regarding ending their own life (see <u>suicide</u> for more details)

* Homicidal ideation: thoughts regarding ending someone else's life

* Assessment

* Ask the patient if they sometimes feel that life is not worth living and if they have ever felt the desire to harm other people.

* Can range from a brief consideration of the act to concrete planning of the time, place, and/or method of <u>suicide</u>/homicide.

* Assess the threat (organized plan, access to weapons).

* Admit the patient involuntarily if they refuse medical care.

* In <u>homicidal</u> threats, inform the authorities and the threatened individual.





### <u>Obsessions</u> and <u>compulsions</u>




* Obsession: A repetitive, persistent, intrusive, and unpleasant thought or urge that causes severe <u>distress</u> and <u>anxiety</u>.

* Compulsion: Ritualistic, repetitive behaviors (e.g., touching, washing) or mental act (e.g., counting, repeating a word silently) carried out in an effort to relieve urges and decrease <u>obsession</u>-related <u>distress</u>.

* Assessment

* Ask the patient if there is something they constantly think about and whether they engage in any specific behavior to get rid of the persistent thoughts

* See <u>obsessive-compulsive disorder</u> for more information.





### Phobias




* A <u>specific phobia</u> is a persistent (≥ 6 months) and intense fear of one or more specific situations or objects (phobic stimuli).

* Some common examples of <u>phobias</u> include <u>agoraphobia</u> (fear of unknown places and situations), <u>claustrophobia</u> (fear of enclosed places), <u>arachnophobia</u> (fear of spiders), and <u>hematophobia</u> (fear of blood).

* Can be assessed by asking the patient whether they are scared of anything and how long this fear has affected them

* See <u>anxiety disorders</u> for more information.

---

## Perceptual disturbances

<u>Perceptual disturbances</u> are characterized by disruption in perception, which may be caused by physical and/or mental disorders.




### Hallucinations




* Definition: <u>perceptual disturbances</u> in which sensory experiences occur in the absence of external stimuli

* Can be assessed by asking the patient if they ever hear, see, feel, <u>smell</u>, or <u>taste</u> things that other individuals do not.

* Some of the most common causes of <u>hallucinations</u> include:

* <u>Substance abuse</u>

* <u>Delirium</u> or <u>dementia</u>

* <u>Epilepsy</u>

* <u>Fever</u> (especially in children and the elderly)

* <u>Narcolepsy</u>

* <u>Schizophrenia</u>

* Sensory impairment (e.g., <u>deafness</u>, blindness)





| <br>Types of <u>hallucinations</u> [[13]](/library/gibFIt) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Description | <u>Epidemiology</u>/etiology |
| Auditory hallucination | <br>* A false perception of sound (e.g., <u>hearing</u> voices)<br><br> | <br><br>* The most common type of <u>hallucination</u><br><br>* Usually seen in psychiatric disorders (e.g., <u>schizophrenia</u>, <u>depression</u> with <u>psychotic features</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Visual hallucination | <br>* A false perception of sight (e.g., seeing faces)<br><br> | <br>* The most common type of <u>hallucination</u> in patients with <u>delirium</u> or <u>dementia</u><br><br> |
| Olfactory hallucination | <br>* A false perception of <u>smell</u>, usually unpleasant (e.g., the <u>smell</u> of burnt or rotten food)<br><br> | <br>* The most common type of <u>hallucination</u> seen in patients with focal-onset <u>temporal lobe seizures</u> (including symptomatic <u>epileptic seizures</u> caused by <u>brain tumors</u>)<br><br> |
| Gustatory hallucination | <br>* A false perception of <u>taste</u>, usually unpleasant (e.g., a metallic <u>taste</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Rare; also associated with <u>aura</u> in focal-onset <u>temporal lobe epilepsy</u><br><br> |
| Somatic (tactile) hallucination | <br>* A false perception of touch (e.g., the sensation of a snake wrapping around one's leg)<br><br> | <br><br>* A common finding in <u>alcohol withdrawal</u> and intoxication with stimulants (e.g., <u>cocaine</u>, <u>amphetamine</u>, <u>methamphetamine</u>)<br><br>* A symptom of <u>delusional parasitosis</u> (e.g., “<u>cocaine</u> crawlies” in <u>cocaine intoxication</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Sleep hallucinations</u> | <br><br>* Vivid, often frightening visual or <u>auditory hallucinations</u> that can be <u>hypnagogic</u> (while going to <u>sleep</u>) or hypnopompic (while waking up)<br><br>* See <u>narcolepsy</u> for more information.<br><br><br> | <br>* See <u>narcolepsy</u> for more information.<br><br> |
| <u>Synesthesia</u> | <br>* Not a type of <u>hallucination</u>, but a <u>perceptual disturbance</u> in which stimulation of one sense produces a sensation related to another sense (e.g., an olfactory stimulus that produces a visual sensation)<br><br> | <br>* N/A<br><br> |





### Illusions




* Definition: <u>perceptual disturbances</u> in which real external stimuli are misinterpreted (e.g., perceiving a stationary object as being in motion)

* Assess by asking the patient whether they sometimes misinterpret real things around them, such as shadows or faint noises

* Similar to <u>hallucinations</u>, <u>illusions</u> can be categorized according to the misinterpreted sensory input as visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, and gustatory.

* Although <u>illusions</u> are characteristic of some mental disorders (e.g., <u>schizophrenia</u>), most <u>illusions</u> are physiological in nature and generated by each individual's perceptive assumptions based on their psychological profile (e.g., influenced by darkness, fatigue, or under the influence of drugs or <u>alcohol</u>).





### <u>Dissociation (psychiatry)</u>




* A psychological <u>defense mechanism</u> that is a natural protective response to a traumatic or stressful experience.

* Characterized by disruption and/or discontinuity of normal consciousness, <u>memory</u>, identity, and perception of oneself (e.g., <u>derealization</u>, <u>depersonalization</u>)

* Can be assessed by asking the patient whether they sometimes feel detached from themselves or others or if the world around them sometimes feels unnatural

* See <u>dissociative disorders</u> for more information.





### Agnosia




* Characterized by impaired recognition of sensory stimulus (most commonly visual) [[14]](/library/t8aXom)

* Can be tested by presenting different objects or exposing a patient to different stimuli (depending on recognition of which modality is tested)

* Can still recognize the objects using different <u>sensory modalities</u> (unless multiple senses affected)

* Types include:

* Visual agnosia: inability to recognize visually presented objects despite otherwise normal <u>vision</u>
* Caused by a lesion in the <u>visual association cortex</u> in the <u>occipital lobe</u> (Brodmann area 19) or <u>ventral</u> visual stream in the <u>temporal lobe</u>

* Auditory agnosia: inability to recognize sounds despite intact <u>hearing</u>
* Caused by lesions of the auditory <u>ventral</u> stream (<u>anterior</u> <u>superior temporal gyrus</u>).

* Tactile agnosia (<u>astereognosis</u>): inability to recognize objects by touch using texture, shape, and temperature as cues without visual input
* Caused by a lesion in the <u>contralateral</u> <u>parietal lobe</u> (areas 5 and 7).

* Visuospatial dysgnosia: inability to localize and orient oneself and/or identify relationships between objects in the environment
* Often associated with damage to the right <u>posterior</u> parietal area of the <u>brain</u>.

* Prosopagnosia: inability to recognize familiar faces, while the ability to name parts of the face (e.g., nose, mouth) or identify individuals by other cues (e.g., clothing, voices) is left intact.
* Caused by bilateral lesions or large unilateral lesions of the <u>ventral</u> occipitotemporal cortex (fusiform <u>gyrus</u>)

* Autotopagnosia: inability to localize different parts of the body upon request
* Caused by damage to left <u>posterior</u> parietal area of the cortex





### Hemineglect (also known as <u>unilateral neglect</u> or <u>spatial neglect</u>)




* <u>Hemineglect</u> is the impaired ability to perceive and respond to different types of stimuli coming from one side of the body usually due to a <u>brain</u> unilateral injury (most commonly <u>strokes</u>).

* Typically associated with right hemisphere damage resulting in neglect (esp. visual) of the left side [[15]](/library/ZCYZqr)

* The lesion is usually <u>contralateral</u> to the side where the perception is absent

* Can be tested by asking to copy a figure, draw the face of a clock, cancel symbols on a paper, etc. An individual with <u>hemineglect</u> is only able to copy the part of the image or cancel symbols on the perceived side.

* Common types:

* Motor neglect

* Sensory or perceptual neglect
